prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

WASHINGTON (CNN) -- Justice Department officials blocked liberals and people with Democratic Party ties from a highly selective program that funneled young lawyers into government jobs, according to an internal investigation released Tuesday. A bias against liberals existed in a Justice program meant to hire young lawyers, an investigation found. Esther Slater McDonald, a political appointee at the Justice Department, "wrote disparaging statements about the candidates' liberal and Democratic Party affiliations on the applications she reviewed and ... she voted to deselect candidates on that basis," said the report by Inspector General Glenn Fine. McDonald, who has left the department, refused to be interviewed for the investigation. The report, the first official investigation to document politicization of the Justice Department during the Bush administration, is an offshoot of the larger investigation of Justice Department politics triggered by the furor over the firing of nine U.S. attorneys. It found two of three members of a screening committee considered political views and experience when choosing new lawyers for the Justice Department Honors Program and Summer Law Intern Program. The report found that McDonald and Michael Elston, the chief of staff to Deputy Attorney General Paul McNulty, engaged in misconduct, an administrative violation. The third member of the screening committee, career lawyer Dan Fridman, was cleared of any involvement in the politicization of the process. Elston was interviewed by the investigators, who asked him about the role of former Justice Department official Monica Goodling in politicizing the selection process. Elston told investigators he could not recall Goodling telling him to select lawyers who appeared to share Attorney General Alberto Gonzales' philosophy. Goodling testified before a House panel last year that she had told Elston he should identify such candidates. Goodling directed Elston to lead the selection committee in 2006. She and Elston have both left the Justice Department. She refused to be interviewed for the inspector general's report. As a result of the controversy, the hiring process was changed in 2007 to insulate hiring decisions from political considerations. Both Justice Department policy and federal law prohibit discrimination in hiring for career positions on the basis of political affiliations. The report did not find clear evidence that an earlier screening committee took political considerations into account. It says data from 2002 shows a disparity in the hiring of liberal and conservative candidates, but there were no complaints about the committee's work from 2003 to 2006, when Goodling put Elston in charge of the process. The report Tuesday is the first of perhaps several to be issued as the broad-ranging investigation into the role partisan politics has played in the Justice Department during the Bush administration. Goodling is expected to be a central figure in later inspector general reports examining efforts to increase the influence of conservatives in the department. The Justice Department Office of Professional Responsibility, a separate watchdog office that monitors prosecutorial conduct, joined in the inspector general's investigation. CNN's Terry Frieden contributed to this report.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a CNN-style news article about an internal Justice Department investigation finding that liberal and Democratic-affiliated applicants were excluded from selective hiring programs during the Bush administration.
counterfactuals.output:
# Justice Department probe finds political bias in Bush-era hiring programs

**WASHINGTON** — An internal Justice Department investigation found that liberal and Democratic-affiliated applicants were improperly screened out of prestigious hiring programs during the George W. Bush administration, according to a report released by the department’s watchdogs.

The investigation concluded that political and ideological considerations influenced decisions involving the Attorney General’s Honors Program and the Summer Law Intern Program, both intended to attract top law students and recent graduates to the department.

Federal law and Justice Department policy prohibit political affiliation from being considered in hiring career employees.

Investigators from the department’s Office of Inspector General and Office of Professional Responsibility examined hiring practices in 2002 and from 2006 to 2007. They found that screening committees in 2002 and 2006 used candidates’ political or ideological affiliations to reject some applicants.

Applicants with ties to Democratic politicians, liberal advocacy groups or organizations viewed as politically opposed to the administration were rejected at substantially higher rates than candidates with conservative affiliations, the report said.

In 2006, investigators found, nearly half of the applicants whose résumés reflected Democratic or liberal connections were eliminated during a centralized screening process. By comparison, only a small fraction of applicants with Republican, conservative or neutral affiliations were rejected.

The report said committee members appeared to rely on résumé entries such as participation in civil rights, environmental or reproductive-rights organizations, as well as work for Democratic officeholders. Applicants with connections to conservative organizations were generally not treated the same way.

Investigators said they did not find sufficient evidence to conclude that senior Justice Department leaders explicitly ordered the political screening. But the report faulted officials for failing to properly oversee the process and for allowing selection criteria to be applied without adequate safeguards.

The watchdogs recommended changes to ensure hiring decisions are documented, reviewed and based solely on professional qualifications. The Justice Department said it had revised the selection process, added training and strengthened oversight of the programs.

The findings added to broader concerns about the politicization of the Justice Department during the Bush administration. Separate investigations examined allegations that political loyalty influenced other personnel decisions, including the hiring of career attorneys and the dismissal of several US attorneys.

The Honors Program is one of the federal government’s most competitive entry-level legal programs and serves as a key route into long-term careers at the Justice Department.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize the inspector general’s report on political discrimination in the Justice Department Honors Program and Summer Law Intern Program, including the roles of Esther Slater McDonald, Michael Elston, and Monica Goodling.
counterfactuals.output:
The Justice Department’s Office of Inspector General and Office of Professional Responsibility issued a joint report in July 2008 examining hiring for the Attorney General’s Honors Program and Summer Law Intern Program, both of which are career, nonpolitical programs.

### Main findings

- Political appointees became involved in screening applicants in 2002 and again in 2006, displacing the traditional career-employee review process.
- In both years, applicants’ political or ideological affiliations were improperly considered. Candidates associated with Democratic politicians, liberal organizations, civil-rights groups, environmental groups, or the American Constitution Society were rejected at substantially higher rates than applicants with conservative or Republican affiliations.
- The reviewers sometimes treated advocacy positions, law-school activities, or public-interest work as evidence that candidates would not faithfully represent the government, even when their academic and professional qualifications were strong.
- The investigators concluded that this use of political and ideological considerations violated Justice Department policy and federal civil-service principles governing career hiring. For 2002, however, incomplete records and conflicting testimony made it difficult to assign responsibility for individual decisions.
- The report found no persuasive evidence that the politically skewed results could be explained simply by merit-based factors such as grades, experience, or writing ability.

### Roles of the three officials

- **Esther Slater McDonald**, then counsel to the associate attorney general, was a central member of the 2006 screening committee. The report found that she considered applicants’ political and ideological affiliations and used them to help decide whom to remove from interview lists. Investigators rejected her explanation that she was merely assessing whether applicants would zealously represent the government.

- **Michael Elston**, then chief of staff to the deputy attorney general, also participated in and helped oversee the 2006 screening. The report concluded that he shared responsibility for the improper process, including approving or acquiescing in deselections affected by political or ideological considerations rather than ensuring that career-hiring standards were followed.

- **Monica Goodling**, the Department’s White House liaison and senior counselor to the attorney general, helped choose the political appointees who served as screeners and was part of the broader effort to give political leadership greater control over hiring. However, the Honors/SLIP investigation did **not** find sufficient evidence that she directed the committee to discriminate or personally made the challenged deselection decisions. A separate inspector-general investigation found that Goodling used political criteria in other career hiring and personnel actions.

### Outcome

The report recommended restoring career officials to the central screening role, adopting clearer written criteria, preserving decision records, training participants on prohibited political considerations, and strengthening oversight. By the time the report was released, the Department had already changed portions of the process, and several officials involved—including McDonald, Elston, and Goodling—had left the Department.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a detailed news report on the politicization of career-lawyer hiring at the U.S. Justice Department, preserving key names, findings, quotations, and subsequent reforms.
counterfactuals.output:
# Justice Department’s career hiring became a political battleground, watchdogs found

**WASHINGTON —** For much of President George W. Bush’s administration, political appointees at the Justice Department improperly used party affiliation and ideology to influence the selection of career lawyers and other nonpolitical employees, according to a series of internal investigations that prompted hiring reforms and became a central chapter in the controversy over the department’s independence.

Reports by the Justice Department’s Office of Inspector General, or OIG, and Office of Professional Responsibility, or OPR, found that applicants with Democratic or liberal affiliations were rejected at disproportionately high rates from prestigious entry-level legal programs. Investigators also concluded that political criteria were used in hiring immigration judges, assistant U.S. attorneys and lawyers in the Civil Rights Division.

The reports did not find that every unsuccessful applicant had been rejected for political reasons, nor did they conclude that all hiring throughout the department was corrupted. But they documented a repeated breakdown of rules intended to insulate career employment decisions from partisan pressure.

Federal personnel law and Justice Department policy generally prohibit officials from discriminating in career hiring on the basis of political affiliation. The watchdogs concluded that several senior officials either violated those restrictions or permitted a process in which improper political considerations could flourish.

## Political appointees take control of entry-level hiring

At the center of the first investigation were the **Attorney General’s Honors Program**, the department’s primary route for hiring entry-level lawyers, and the **Summer Law Intern Program**, commonly called SLIP.

Before 2002, career lawyers in the department’s divisions and offices played the principal role in evaluating applicants. The Bush Justice Department changed that system, giving political appointees in the Office of the Attorney General a much larger role in screening candidates and deciding who would receive interviews.

The new process drew particular scrutiny during the 2006 hiring cycle. Career officials initially selected applicants for interviews, but a screening committee composed largely of political appointees then removed significant numbers of candidates from consideration. The committee’s decisions often lacked a clear written explanation, leaving investigators to compare the applications, interview lists and evidence of political or ideological activity.

In a June 2008 report, the OIG and OPR concluded that applicants whose résumés showed Democratic Party work, liberal advocacy or affiliations with organizations viewed as left-leaning were rejected at a “significantly higher rate” than applicants with Republican, conservative or neutral backgrounds.

The investigators said the pattern could not be adequately explained by grades, law-school ranking or other traditional qualifications. Some applicants with strong academic records and prestigious clerkships were removed, while candidates with visible Republican or conservative credentials generally fared better.

The report concluded:

> “The evidence in our investigation showed that political or ideological affiliations were used to deselect candidates in both the Honors Program and SLIP in 2006.”

The watchdogs said the conduct violated Justice Department policy and federal law governing merit-based career hiring.

## Esther Slater McDonald and the 2006 screening process

One of the principal figures in the 2006 review was **Esther Slater McDonald**, counsel to Associate Attorney General **William Mercer**. McDonald participated in screening candidates and conducted Internet searches that could reveal political activities not apparent from their applications.

Investigators found that she searched for information about applicants’ organizational ties, political contributions and public activities. They concluded that her decisions reflected political and ideological judgments, although McDonald disputed that characterization and said she was looking for evidence of judgment, commitment and suitability for Justice Department work.

The report found that other committee members did not always share her reasoning and that the process had few safeguards. Screening decisions were not consistently documented, and career components were often given little or no explanation for why candidates they had chosen were removed.

Political appointees involved in earlier hiring cycles included **Michael Elston**, then chief of staff to Deputy Attorney General **Paul McNulty**. The investigators found evidence of political consideration in the 2002 and 2006 processes, though gaps in records prevented them from making equally definitive findings about every intervening year.

The watchdogs stressed that the centralized system itself was not necessarily unlawful. The problem was that political appointees used, or appeared to use, criteria that were forbidden in selecting career employees.

## Monica Goodling and the broader hiring scandal

A separate OIG-OPR investigation focused on **Monica Goodling**, the Justice Department’s White House liaison and senior counsel to Attorney General **Alberto Gonzales**.

Goodling had broad influence over political appointments, but investigators found that she also assessed political loyalties when considering candidates for positions that were supposed to be career or otherwise nonpartisan. Those positions included immigration judges, members of the Board of Immigration Appeals, assistant U.S. attorneys and other departmental jobs.

Witnesses said Goodling asked applicants questions such as:

> “What is it about George W. Bush that makes you want to serve him?”

She also asked some candidates about their political philosophy, voting history or views on abortion and other politically charged subjects, according to the investigation.

Goodling, testifying before the House Judiciary Committee in 2007 under a grant of immunity, acknowledged that she had improperly taken political considerations into account:

> “I know I crossed the line.”

In July 2008, the OIG and OPR concluded that Goodling had “violated federal law and Department policy” by using political or ideological affiliations in hiring for career positions.

The report also criticized **Kyle Sampson**, Gonzales’s former chief of staff, particularly for his role in the selection of immigration judges. Although immigration judges are appointed by the attorney general and historically had been handled differently from ordinary civil-service jobs, the department had treated them as career positions. The investigators found that political recommendations and White House connections had nevertheless become important factors.

Goodling’s White House liaison office maintained lists and sought candidates through Republican political networks. In some cases, department officials gave favorable treatment to people recommended by the White House, Republican officeholders or conservative organizations.

The investigators said this was not simply a matter of political appointees preferring like-minded colleagues for policymaking posts. The positions at issue were designated as career jobs and therefore were not supposed to be filled on a partisan basis.

## Civil Rights Division favored “right-thinking Americans”

The scrutiny extended to the Justice Department’s **Civil Rights Division**, where political appointees had assumed greater control over the hiring of career lawyers.

A January 2009 OIG-OPR report focused on **Bradley Schlozman**, who served in senior Civil Rights Division posts and later as interim U.S. attorney in Missouri. Investigators found that Schlozman and others considered applicants’ political and ideological backgrounds in hiring and personnel decisions.

Schlozman was described by witnesses as seeking “**right-thinking Americans**” for the division. Emails and testimony showed that he used disparaging terms for liberal lawyers, including “**commies**” and “**pinkos**,” while praising conservative applicants.

The report concluded that Schlozman had violated federal law and Justice Department policy by considering political and ideological affiliations in hiring career attorneys. It also found that he had made false statements in sworn testimony to Congress when he denied that he had taken such factors into account.

Schlozman disputed important parts of the report and maintained that he had been seeking lawyers committed to enforcing the administration’s civil-rights priorities rather than applying a political test.

The matter was referred for possible prosecution. Federal prosecutors ultimately declined to bring criminal charges, a result that underscored the difference between an administrative finding of misconduct and proof sufficient for a criminal case.

## Damage to the department’s credibility

The hiring investigations unfolded alongside the controversy over the 2006 dismissal of nine U.S. attorneys. Although U.S. attorneys are political appointees and may be removed by the president, the scandal exposed the unusually close role played by the White House and political staff in Justice Department personnel decisions.

The combined controversies led to the resignations of Gonzales, Goodling, Sampson and other senior officials. They also intensified congressional concern that political appointees were blurring the line between legitimate control of administration policy and improper interference with professional law enforcement.

Career lawyers told investigators that the hiring practices damaged morale and created a perception that advancement depended on ideological compatibility. The effects were potentially long-lasting: Honors Program lawyers often remain at the department for years and can become senior prosecutors, litigators and managers.

The watchdogs also found that weak recordkeeping made accountability difficult. Applications were annotated inconsistently, explanations for rejections were often missing, and some officials said they could not remember why particular candidates had been removed. That meant investigators could identify broad statistical patterns and specific examples but could not reconstruct every decision.

## Reforms returned authority to career officials

The Justice Department began revising the system before all of the watchdog reports were complete.

Under Attorney General **Michael Mukasey**, who succeeded Gonzales in November 2007, the department adopted measures intended to restore merit-based hiring and prevent political appointees from screening candidates according to party or ideology.

The reforms included:

- returning a larger and more clearly defined role to career lawyers in selecting Honors Program and summer-intern candidates;
- limiting political-appointee participation in career hiring;
- requiring written, job-related criteria for screening applicants;
- documenting the reasons candidates were accepted or rejected;
- training officials on prohibited personnel practices;
- reinforcing the ban on considering political affiliation in career employment;
- increasing review by the Office of the Deputy Attorney General and departmental ethics and personnel officials; and
- separating the White House liaison’s political-appointments work from career hiring.

The department also changed the process for selecting immigration judges and Board of Immigration Appeals members. Vacancies were publicly announced, applicants were evaluated through more standardized procedures, and career officials were given a formal role in screening and interviewing candidates.

The watchdogs recommended continuing audits and oversight, warning that written rules would be ineffective without records sufficient to show how decisions had been made.

## A lasting lesson about political control

The investigations drew an important distinction: presidents and attorneys general are entitled to appoint political officials who share their priorities, and those officials may direct the department’s policies within the law. But career lawyers, immigration judges and other permanent employees are not supposed to be selected according to partisan loyalty.

The Bush-era cases showed how quickly that boundary could erode when political staff controlled applications, searched candidates’ backgrounds and made unexplained decisions without meaningful career review.

The subsequent reforms were designed to rebuild that boundary. Yet the episode has continued to resonate whenever administrations seek greater control over the Justice Department’s permanent workforce. The central finding of the watchdog reports remains the same: political leadership may set policy, but career hiring must rest on professional qualifications rather than party allegiance or ideology.
